# Identification and mediation: what the design lets the data answer {#sec-identification}

In the north of the Netherlands, decades of gas extraction have caused earthquakes, and the people who live above the gas field vote differently from the rest of the country. Researchers who surveyed the region proposed a chain of explanations [@otjes2020]: experiencing earthquakes erodes trust in the national government, feeds a sense of injustice, and strengthens regional identification, and each of these in turn pushes people toward a protest vote. @fig-otjes draws the claim. The theory does not stop at "earthquakes cause protest voting"; it says the effect runs *through* something. Questions of this shape are called **mediation** questions, and the social and health sciences ask them constantly, because a mechanism is what a theory is made of, and because a mediator suggests a lever: if distrust carries the effect, restoring trust might interrupt it.

![The protest-voting theory of @otjes2020 as a path diagram: earthquake experience works on the protest vote through several parallel mediators.](diagrams/otjes.png){#fig-otjes width="85%" fig-align="center"}

Mediation illustrates a larger problem, and that problem is the subject of this chapter. The last chapter warned that a model which fits the data is not thereby true. The hard version of the warning is that some questions cannot be settled by any amount of data, because the design never put the answer into the data in the first place. Statisticians call this the problem of "identification". Identification is a limit on knowledge set by the design, not by the sample size.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false" title="Optional in this chapter"}
Modern mediation analysis: counterfactual definitions (what an indirect effect means when the model has interactions or a binary outcome; Exercise 3.7 belongs to it). Everything else is required, as are all other inline exercises.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false" title="Before you start"}
This chapter uses four results from earlier chapters: the practice model $\xi \to \eta_1 \to \eta_2$ and its notation (@sec-graph-to-equations); the decomposition rule, which writes each correlation as a sum of paths (@def-decomposition); the hand solution of the three-variable model and the chi-square test of a restriction (@sec-estimating-testing); and the threats to validity and the designs that answer them (@sec-validity, @sec-designs).
:::

## The cross-sectional mediation model {#sec-mediation-model}

The recipe of @sec-theory-to-glm turns the simplest mediation theory into two equations. In the notation of that chapter, the cause is exogenous, so it is written $\xi$; the mediator and the outcome are endogenous, $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$. With all three variables standardized:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= \gamma_1\,\xi + \zeta_1 \\
\eta_2 &= \beta\,\eta_1 + \gamma_2\,\xi + \zeta_2 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mediation}

This is the practice model of @sec-theory-to-glm, and the decomposition rule gives the property that makes mediation attractive. Two relationships connect $\xi$ and $\eta_2$: the direct effect, which contributes $\gamma_2$, and an indirect effect through the mediator, which contributes $\gamma_1 \beta$. Their sum is the total effect, and here, only because nothing in this model is a common cause of $\xi$ and $\eta_2$, that sum is also the implied correlation. Estimating the two equations and multiplying yields "the share of the effect that runs through the mediator".^[This estimation recipe has circulated in psychology for decades under the name of @baron1986. Baron and Kenny write the path into the mediator as $a$, the path out of it as $b$, the direct effect as $c'$ and the indirect effect as the product $ab$; in this book's notation these are $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_1\beta$. Published papers, and Exercises 3.B and 7.6, use the $ab$ notation. Whether the estimates come from the Baron–Kenny regressions, from `lavaan` or from a macro such as PROCESS, they are the same numbers. My subject is what the numbers mean, not how to compute them.]

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.1"}
In a study of education ($\xi$), health knowledge ($\eta_1$), and longevity ($\eta_2$), the estimates are $\hat\gamma_1 = 0.5$, $\hat\beta = 0.4$, $\hat\gamma_2 = 0.1$. Compute the indirect, direct, and total effects and the proportion mediated. Then state in one sentence what the indirect effect claims about the world, if the model is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.1"}
Indirect $= 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.20$; direct $= 0.10$; total $= 0.30$; proportion mediated $= 0.20/0.30 = 2/3$. The claim: two thirds of education's benefit for longevity arises because education raises health knowledge, which raises longevity, so an intervention on health knowledge alone could capture most of the benefit. That is a strong claim, and the rest of the chapter asks what would justify it.
:::

## The assumptions behind the arrows {#sec-mediation-assumptions}

Equations [-@eq-mediation] are claims, and their credibility rests on assumptions. To read $\hat\gamma_1$, $\hat\beta$, and $\hat\gamma_2$ causally you must grant, beyond linearity and additivity: that nothing confounds the cause and the mediator; that nothing confounds the mediator and the outcome, so that $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ are uncorrelated; and that the arrows point the way drawn.

Randomizing $\xi$, the strongest design feature available, secures the first assumption outright, because a coin flip shares no common causes with anything. It secures nothing for the other two, because nobody randomized the mediator. Within each arm of a randomized experiment, the people with high mediator values are different people from the people with low values, and whatever makes them different may drive the outcome on its own. The $\beta$ path is an observational study inside the experiment. Methodologists have said this for years: the mediator-outcome assumption "is needed even in the randomized trial context because, in a trial, although the exposure has been randomized, the mediator typically has not been" [@vanderweele2016]. In one randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy, a naive mediation analysis of antidepressant use made the antidepressants look harmful; VanderWeele concludes that "we get nonsense from the traditional approach if we ignore mediator-outcome confounding".

The next two sections show these failures happening in simulated data, where the truth is known and the failure can be watched directly.

## Failure one: the arrows can be backwards {#sec-failure-reversed}

The first simulation builds a world in which the mediation model is exactly true: the cause raises the mediator ($\gamma_1 = 0.5$), the mediator raises the outcome ($\beta = 0.7$), and no direct effect exists. Two models are then fitted to this world: the true chain, and the same chain with every arrow reversed.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(lavaan)
set.seed(21)
n  <- 10000
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- 0.5 * x1 + rnorm(n)
x3 <- 0.7 * x2 + rnorm(n)
d  <- data.frame(x1, x2, x3)

fit_chain    <- sem("x2 ~ x1 \n x3 ~ x2", data = d)
fit_reversed <- sem("x1 ~ x2 \n x2 ~ x3", data = d)
c(chain = fitMeasures(fit_chain, "chisq"),
  reversed = fitMeasures(fit_reversed, "chisq"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   chain.chisq reversed.chisq 
   0.007331669    0.007331669 
```


:::
:::


The simulation builds the world; the two `sem()` calls fit the rival stories; the last line prints their fit statistics. The statistics agree to every decimal, in this dataset and in every other.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.2"}
(a) Change the two parameter values in the simulation above (for example, replace 0.5 and 0.7 by values of your own), rerun the code, and compare the two chi-square statistics. What changes, and what does not?
(b) Explain the result using the decomposition rule. What does each model imply about the three correlations among $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$?
(c) Then check a third story: fit the model in which $x_3$ causes both $x_1$ and $x_2$ (`"x1 ~ x3 \n x2 ~ x3"`). Does it also fit identically? Why (not)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.2"}
(a) The chi-square values change, because they depend on the simulated data. But the two models' chi-squares remain identical to every decimal, whatever values you choose. The equivalence is a property of the two *models*, not of particular parameter values: for every dataset, each model can fit exactly as well as the other.
(b) Both chains imply the same single restriction. The forward chain implies $\rho_{13} = \rho_{12}\,\rho_{23}$, since the only relationship between $x_1$ and $x_3$ is the indirect effect through $x_2$; the reversed chain implies $\rho_{13} = \rho_{23}\,\rho_{12}$, the same equation. Models that imply identical restrictions on the observable correlations cannot be told apart by any data.
(c) The common-cause story is different: it implies $\rho_{12} = \rho_{13}\,\rho_{23}$, a restriction that is false in this world, so its fit is visibly worse. Fit can eliminate some rivals, but it cannot determine the direction of the chain.^[With nonlinear relationships or non-normal variables the tie can sometimes be broken, because a reversed nonlinear relationship leaves traces in the distributions. Under linearity and normality the equivalence is exact.]
:::

::: {#def-identification}
## Identification
Two models, or two parameter values, are **equivalent** when they imply the same distribution of observable data. A question is **identified** when the distribution of the observable data determines its answer. The question of which of two equivalent models or parameter values is correct is therefore not identified: the data cannot decide it, however many of them you collect. A model with more parameters than observed variances and covariances cannot be identified, but this counting rule is only a necessary condition.
:::

The reversed chain passes the counting rule while the direction stays unidentifiable. Design, unlike fit, can break the tie. If $x_1$ was randomized, an arrow into $x_1$ is absurd, because nothing in the system causes a coin flip; the reversed chain is ruled out by design, not by fit. The earthquake study uses the same logic in weaker form: earthquakes shake houses, and opinions cannot cause earthquakes, so the causal order of the exposure is secure. For the mediator-outcome pair, nothing is secure: distrust may drive protest votes, or a protest identity may feed distrust, and the survey cannot tell.

## Failure two: the hidden confounder {#sec-failure-confounder}

The second simulation violates the second assumption. In a new world, the cause still raises the mediator ($\gamma_1 = 0.5$), but the mediator does nothing to the outcome. An unmeasured variable $U$ drives both mediator and outcome instead. Suppose the variables are a randomized encouragement to study ($X$), study time ($M$), test scores ($Y$), and conscientiousness ($U$).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(5)
n <- 10000
X <- rnorm(n)
U <- rnorm(n) # never measured
# the disturbance sd's keep M and Y at variance 1 (variance rule)
M <- 0.5 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.25 - 0.36))
Y <- 0.0 * M + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.36))
d2 <- data.frame(X, M, Y) # does not include U  :(

round(coef(sem("M ~ X \n Y ~ M + X", data = d2)), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  M~X   Y~M   Y~X  M~~M  Y~~Y 
 0.51  0.47 -0.25  0.77  0.84 
```


:::
:::


The mediation analysis reports a highly significant $\hat\beta$ of about 0.5, which a reader might take as evidence that studying strongly improves scores and that the encouragement works through study time. The estimates are precise, and as causal claims they are wrong: in this world, forcing students to study more would achieve nothing, because study time does not cause scores. Conscientiousness makes the two correlated within each arm of the experiment. The estimated direct effect is also spuriously *negative*. More data would only tighten the intervals around the wrong values. This is @fig-confounding again, with one difference: there the confounded variable was the treatment, which randomization fixed, whereas here the confounded variable is the mediator, which randomization does not reach.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.3"}
Explain, with a trace through the diagram $X \rightarrow M \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$, why the regression of $Y$ on $M$ and $X$ produces a nonzero coefficient on $M$ although $M$ does not cause $Y$. Then explain why randomizing $X$ did not protect us.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.3"}
$M$ and $Y$ share the common cause $U$: high-$U$ students study more and also score higher, so $M$ and $Y$ are correlated at every level of $X$. Regression can only redescribe that correlation, and it attributes the association to the $M$ coefficient. In model terms, $U$ sits inside both $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$, so the disturbances are correlated, violating the no-confounding assumption. Randomization guarantees that $U$ is unrelated to $X$, which is why $\hat\gamma_1$ and the total effect remain correct: by the decomposition rule, $\rho_{XM} = \gamma_1$ and $\rho_{XY} = \gamma_1\beta + \gamma_2$, and neither equation contains the disturbance covariance, because no path from $X$ to $M$ or $Y$ runs through $U$. Randomization constrains nothing about $U$'s relation to $M$ or $Y$, because it protects only the variable it assigned.
:::

## Trading one assumption for another: instrumental variables {#sec-iv}

If we believe there is unmeasured confounding, then this belief should be reflected in the model, as a covariance between the disturbance terms.

With a direct path from $\xi$ to $\eta_2$ still in the model, the unknowns are $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, $\gamma_2$, and the disturbance covariance $\psi$ (the observed variables are standardized, the disturbances are not): four parameters and only three observable correlations, so the model is not identified, and this time the counting rule alone settles it. But suppose the theory can credibly assert that there is *no direct path*, that $\xi$ reaches $\eta_2$ only through $\eta_1$. @fig-iv draws that model. The parameters now number three, and the decomposition rule gives three equations:

![The confounded mediation model. The curved arrow between the disturbances represents unmeasured common causes of mediator and outcome. There is no direct path from the cause to the outcome.](diagrams/mediation.png){#fig-iv width="70%" fig-align="center"}

$$
\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1, \qquad
\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = \beta + \psi, \qquad
\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\,\beta .
$$

The middle equation says the naive mediator-outcome correlation is contaminated: it contains $\beta$ plus a contribution from the correlated disturbances. The other two equations do not contain $\psi$ at all, because no relationship between $\xi$ and either endogenous variable runs through the curved arrow. So we can solve for the target of interest, $\beta$, by dividing the third equation by the first:

$$
\beta = \frac{\rho_{\xi\eta_2}}{\rho_{\xi\eta_1}} .
$$

The causal effect of the mediator is identified *without assuming away the confounding*; $\psi$ has become just another parameter for the data to estimate. The assumption "no mediator-outcome confounding" has been traded for the assumption "no direct effect", which in this role is called the **exclusion restriction**. Neither assumption is testable from these data, because the model that contains both the direct path and the disturbance covariance is not identified; the trade rests entirely on theory. (@sec-mediation-panel shows the one way to test one of the two, which is to assume the other.) When the theory is credible, $\xi$ is called an **instrumental variable** [@angrist1996]: it is no longer of interest for its own sake, but because its randomness moves the mediator, which makes the mediator's effect on the outcome visible.

Applied to the same dataset that misled the mediation analysis:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_iv <- "
  M ~ a * X
  Y ~ b * M
  M ~~ Y        # correlated disturbances: confounding allowed
"
round(coef(sem(model_iv, data = d2))[c("a", "b")], 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    a     b 
 0.51 -0.02 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(cov(d2$X, d2$Y) / cov(d2$X, d2$M), 2)   # the same, by hand
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -0.02
```


:::
:::


The estimate recovers the truth from confounded data: studying does nothing. The second line shows that the estimator is a single division. The formula above divides correlations and the code divides covariances: the covariance ratio estimates the unstandardized effect and the correlation ratio the standardized one, and the two are equal when the mediator and the outcome have the same standard deviation, which holds here because the simulation gave both a variance of 1. This ratio is the **Wald estimator** of instrumental-variable analysis; with several instruments, or with covariates, the same idea becomes **two-stage least squares**, and `lavaan` with correlated disturbances estimates the same quantity.

@sec-rq-to-interpretation already did this division by hand. The Oregon arithmetic, where an effect on those drawn in the lottery was divided by a 25-point rise in coverage, is the same ratio $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$ in a different notation. The numerator is called the **intention-to-treat** effect, and the assumption that licensed the division was the exclusion restriction.

Suppose we observe $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = 0.3$, $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = 0.7$, and $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = 0.15$. The instrumental-variable estimate is $\beta = 0.15/0.3 = 0.5$. The naive estimate, the raw mediator-outcome correlation, is $0.7$. The difference, $0.2$, is confounding that the naive analysis counted as causation.

The estimator depends on three conditions, each of which fails regularly in practice.

*Relevance.* The recipe divides by $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$. If the instrument barely moves the mediator, the division amplifies noise; if $\gamma_1 = 0$, there is nothing to divide by at all. Weak instruments not only widen intervals but make the estimator erratic, as the next exercise shows, and, when the instrument is even slightly invalid, badly biased [@bound1995].

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.4"}
The function below simulates one instrumental-variable study with $n = 1{,}000$, in a world where the true effect of the mediator is zero, and returns the IV estimate. The argument `g1` is the strength of the instrument.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
one_iv <- function(g1) {
  U <- rnorm(1000)
  X <- rnorm(1000)
  M <- g1 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)
  Y <- 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)     # the true effect of M on Y is zero
  cov(X, Y) / cov(X, M)
}
```
:::


(a) Run `replicate(500, one_iv(0.5))` to simulate 500 studies with a strong instrument, and look at the estimates with `summary()`. Around which value do they concentrate, and how far out do the most extreme estimates lie?
(b) Do the same with a weak instrument, `one_iv(0.05)`. Compare the two summaries.
(c) Explain what the division by `cov(X, M)` has to do with the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.4"}
(a) The strong-instrument estimates concentrate tightly around the true value 0; across 500 studies they typically stay within about $\pm 0.2$.
(b) The weak-instrument estimates are wild: most lie further from zero than the *worst* strong-instrument estimate, more than a quarter lie beyond $\pm 1$, and individual studies can return estimates in the tens, of either sign.
(c) The IV estimate divides by the sample covariance between instrument and mediator. With `g1 = 0.05` the true covariance is barely different from zero, so in any one sample the estimated covariance can come out close to zero, or on the wrong side of it, and dividing by a near-zero number produces an estimate that is huge and of unpredictable sign. The information about $\beta$ that the instrument carries shrinks with $\gamma_1$, and at $\gamma_1 = 0$ it is gone entirely.
:::

*Exclusion.* The restriction "no direct path" did real work in the algebra: it removed the direct effect from $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}$, leaving only $\gamma_1\beta$. If a direct path exists after all, the numerator contains $\gamma_1\beta + \gamma_2$, and the ratio delivers a corrupted answer. The data cannot check this, because the model with the direct path was never identified in the first place.

*Exogeneity.* $\xi$ itself must be unconfounded with the outcome, which randomization guarantees and which some naturally occurring variables also satisfy.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.5"}
Work through the full identification argument yourself, in the steps the algebra suggests. (a) Using the decomposition rule on @fig-iv, write the three implied correlations in terms of $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, and $\psi$. (Hint: the joint-effect contribution to $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2}$ that uses the curved arrow may be written simply as "$+$ confounding".) (b) Which two equations identify $\beta$, and why is the third not needed? (c) What goes wrong if we never observed $\xi$ and wanted $\beta$ from the mediator-outcome data alone? (d) What goes wrong if $\gamma_1 = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.5"}
(a) $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$; $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta$; $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = \beta + \text{confounding}$. (b) The first two: $\beta = \rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$. They are the equations free of $\psi$. The third equation is then left over to *estimate* the confounding rather than to assume it away. (c) With only the mediator and the outcome you have one correlation and two unknowns, $\beta$ and the confounding; not identified, which is the ordinary observational predicament. (d) Division by zero: with an irrelevant instrument the data contain no information about $\beta$, and in finite samples a nearly-zero $\gamma_1$ produces the wild estimates of Exercise 3.4.
:::

## Instrumental variables in practice {#sec-iv-practice}

Sometimes nature provides a credible instrument. @hanandita2014 wanted the effect of poverty on mental health in Indonesia, where the naive association is confounded: illness also causes poverty, and many things cause both. Their instrument is rainfall: rainfall anomalies across 440 districts shift household consumption, and a rainfall shock should affect mental health only through the economic hardship it causes. With $N = 577{,}548$, relevance is checkable and strong, exogeneity is argued from meteorology, and, as usual, the exclusion restriction is the debatable clause.^[It is not airtight. Floods can destroy more than income: homes, and occasionally family members, are direct paths from rainfall to distress that bypass consumption. Every instrumental-variable argument has a clause like this, and the paper's robustness checks are aimed at it.] Their estimate: halving consumption raises the probability of mental illness by 0.06, about five times the naive association, which measurement error in consumption had attenuated. Random error in a predictor pulls its regression coefficient toward zero, a bias called **attenuation**; an instrument is immune to it, because it uses only the part of consumption that rainfall moves, and that is why an IV estimate can be larger than the naive one.

Sometimes we build the instrument. An **encouragement design** randomizes not the behaviour itself but an invitation to it, then uses the randomized invitation as an instrument for the behaviour [@holland1988]. The same logic applies to any trial with imperfect compliance: assignment is randomized, treatment received is not, and assignment instruments treatment received. In the JOBS II trial for unemployed workers, only some of those assigned to job-search workshops attended, so assignment served as the instrument for participation [@tingley2014].

Sometimes the instrument is genetic. **Mendelian randomization** uses genetic variants as instruments: a variant that raises alcohol consumption is dealt out at conception, plausibly independent of later confounders, and instruments the effect of drinking on, say, esophageal cancer [@daveysmith2003]. The threat to exclusion here has its own name, "pleiotropy", one gene working through many pathways, and modern practice is largely a set of partial defenses against it [@davies2018].

Instrumental variables are widely used in economics, above all for evaluating policies. The classic is Angrist and Krueger's quarter-of-birth instrument: compulsory-schooling laws force children born early in the year to stay in school slightly longer, and that small amount of law-induced schooling instruments the effect of education on earnings [@angrist1991]. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, which @sec-rq-to-interpretation introduced, is a modern policy example: the lottery is the randomized instrument, Medicaid enrollment the treatment it moves, and the division you did there is the IV estimate of Medicaid's effect on health and finances [@finkelstein2012; @baicker2013]. In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, families in high-poverty housing projects were randomized to receive housing vouchers, but only some moved; using the voucher as an instrument for moving, children who moved before age 13 earned 31 percent more as adults than controls, a finding that reshaped American housing policy [@chetty2016]. And a design now common in applied economics uses institutional randomness as the instrument: in Norway, criminal cases are assigned to judges of measurably different strictness, so the assigned judge's leniency instruments incarceration itself; incarceration turned out to *reduce* reoffending, by 29 percentage points over five years, where the naive comparison had suggested the opposite [@bhuller2020].

Each of these designs inherits the three conditions in its own form, and the standard criticisms of instrumental variables are doubts about those conditions. Economists learned that celebrated instruments can be weak; the quarter-of-birth instrument is the canonical case [@bound1995]. A subtler criticism: even a valid instrument answers a narrower question than the one usually asked, because it estimates the effect among the **compliers**, the units whose treatment or mediator value the instrument actually changed. In an encouragement design the compliers are the people who take up the behaviour when invited and would not have taken it up otherwise; people who would have done it regardless, or never, contribute nothing to the estimate, so the IV estimate is an average effect over the compliers only, called the **local average treatment effect** [@angrist1996]. Critics like @deaton2010 ask whether that local effect was the question anyone posed. Mediation analysis in psychology has its own list of criticisms: mediators measured minutes before outcomes, assumptions unstated, and a literature of causal-sounding conclusions resting on the naive $\beta$ path [@bullock2010; @rohrer2022]. The remedy is to keep the how-question but treat the mediation model as this book treats every model: as a set of assumptions that the design must justify.

## Mediation over time: the Yang model on panel data {#sec-mediation-panel}

Time is a design resource for mediation. A mediation theory is a claim about a process: the cause changes the mediator, and the changed mediator later changes the outcome. Measuring the three variables in that order, in separate waves of a panel, does two things at once. It secures part of failure one, because an arrow running backwards in time is absurd for the same reason an arrow into a coin flip is. And it takes the theory's own dynamics seriously: when the true process unfolds over time, cross-sectional mediation estimates are not just imprecise but systematically biased for the longitudinal parameters they are read as [@maxwell2007], and the standard repair is to measure the cause, the mediator, and the outcome at successive waves [@cole2003]. Temporal ordering does nothing for failure two: nobody randomized the mediator in a panel either, and unmeasured common causes of mediator and outcome are as dangerous across waves as within one.

The LISS panel repeats both questionnaires of @sec-theory-to-glm every year, so the full Yang model can be taken to panel data. LISS is run by Centerdata and is part of ODISSEI, the Dutch national research infrastructure for the social sciences (<https://odissei-data.nl>), which also gives researchers access to the registers of Statistics Netherlands. Three annual waves (2023, 2024, 2025) give the temporally ordered version: social integration in 2023, the two measurable physiological states, hypertension and BMI, in 2024, and the count of other diagnosed conditions in 2025, with the states' disturbances correlated and, as the theory demands, no direct path from integration to disease.^[The analysis file is built from waves 16-18 of the LISS Health and Social Integration studies by `analysis/liss/03-longitudinal-yang.R` in the book's repository, with the same variable construction as @sec-theory-to-glm in every wave. The models use full-information maximum likelihood, so all 6,467 adults observed in at least one wave contribute.] Three options in the `sem()` call below need a word. `missing = "fiml"` is full-information maximum likelihood: every respondent observed in at least one wave contributes, under the assumption that whether a value is missing does not depend on the value itself once the observed variables are taken into account. `estimator = "MLR"` makes the standard errors and the chi-square robust to non-normal variables such as a 0/1 diagnosis. `fixed.x = FALSE` treats the exogenous variable as random, so that its covariances with the others are part of the model and its missing values are handled too.^[The LISS microdata cannot be redistributed, so this chunk cannot be run from the repository as it stands. A synthetic stand-in with the same variables, simulated from the models fitted to the real data, is shipped as `data-synthetic/liss_yang_longitudinal_synthetic.csv` (see `data-synthetic/README.md`); replace the `readRDS(...)` line by `read.csv("data-synthetic/liss_yang_longitudinal_synthetic.csv")` to run the code yourself. Its numbers differ somewhat from the ones printed here.]


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(lavaan)
liss <- readRDS("../data/liss-health-social-integration/liss_yang_longitudinal.rds")
m3 <- "
  hypertension_17  ~ g1 * integration_16
  bmi_17           ~ g2 * integration_16
  disease_count_18 ~ b1 * hypertension_17 + b2 * bmi_17
  hypertension_17 ~~ psi * bmi_17
"
fit3 <- sem(m3, data = liss, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
            fixed.x = FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit3, c("ntotal", "chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "pvalue.scaled"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       ntotal  chisq.scaled     df.scaled pvalue.scaled 
     6467.000         0.358         1.000         0.550 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
standardizedSolution(fit3)[1:5, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
               lhs op             rhs est.std    se pvalue
1  hypertension_17  ~  integration_16  -0.005 0.015  0.724
2           bmi_17  ~  integration_16  -0.057 0.014  0.000
3 disease_count_18  ~ hypertension_17   0.293 0.017  0.000
4 disease_count_18  ~          bmi_17   0.104 0.015  0.000
5  hypertension_17 ~~          bmi_17   0.153 0.014  0.000
```


:::
:::


The exclusion restriction passes: one degree of freedom, chi-square 0.36, $p = .55$. @sec-iv said that the exclusion restriction is not testable, and here it is being tested; the difference is in what else the model assumes. This model fixes the covariances between the disturbances of the two states and the disturbance of the disease count at zero, that is, it assumes no confounding of the mediator-outcome paths, so the direct path is the only parameter left out and the one leftover degree of freedom tests it. Free those disturbance covariances instead, as the instrumental-variable model did, and the degree of freedom is spent on confounding and the test disappears (with two mediators there are two such covariances, more than one degree of freedom can pay for). Either restriction can be tested only by assuming the other. The estimates say that integration in one year predicts lower BMI the next ($-.06$), that it barely predicts the hypertension diagnosis, and that both states predict the later disease count (.29 and .10). A two-wave version, integration in 2024 predicting states and disease in 2025, gives nearly identical numbers. That is a warning sign: if putting a year between the variables changes nothing, the estimates may not describe what happens over a year.

This can be tested by letting each variable control its own past, the longitudinal design of @cole2003: each 2024 state is regressed on its own 2023 value as well as on integration, and the 2025 disease count on its own 2023 value as well as on the states. The arrow from a variable to itself one wave later is called an **autoregressive** path.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m3ar <- "
  hypertension_17  ~ g1 * integration_16 + a1 * hypertension_16
  bmi_17           ~ g2 * integration_16 + a2 * bmi_16
  disease_count_18 ~ b1 * hypertension_17 + b2 * bmi_17 +
                     a3 * disease_count_16
  hypertension_17 ~~ psi * bmi_17
"
fit3ar <- sem(m3ar, data = liss, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
              fixed.x = FALSE)
s <- standardizedSolution(fit3ar)
s[s$op == "~", c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
               lhs              rhs est.std    se pvalue
1  hypertension_17   integration_16   0.000 0.007  0.964
2  hypertension_17  hypertension_16   0.900 0.009  0.000
3           bmi_17   integration_16  -0.019 0.005  0.000
4           bmi_17           bmi_16   0.911 0.014  0.000
5 disease_count_18  hypertension_17   0.052 0.010  0.000
6 disease_count_18           bmi_17   0.033 0.010  0.001
7 disease_count_18 disease_count_16   0.824 0.009  0.000
```


:::
:::


The structural paths almost disappear. The autoregressive paths are very large, .82 to .91, because a diagnosis, once given, stays: these outcomes are cumulative stocks, and year-to-year change in them is rare. What is left after controlling the past is the model's answer to a different and better-matched question, whether integration predicts *changes* in the states and whether those changes predict *changes* in disease. It barely does: integration still predicts BMI change ($-.019$, small but reliable), the state-change paths shrink to .05 and .03, and the total indirect effect falls from $-.008$ to about $-.001$. Most of what the first model reported was stable between-person differences described twice, not a process unfolding over time, which is the bias @maxwell2007 warned that cross-sectional habits of reading impose on longitudinal questions.

The fuller analysis gives two further results.^[The complete set of models, including the two-wave version, is in `analysis/liss/liss-longitudinal-report.md` in the book's repository.] First, adding age and sex to the three-wave model uncovers a **suppression** pattern, an effect hidden in the raw association because a confounder pushes in the opposite direction: integration's path to hypertension, invisible in the raw model, emerges at $-.034$ ($p = .016$) once age is held constant, because age raises both organizational involvement and blood pressure. Second, with the controls in place the exclusion test gives a borderline rejection ($\chi^2(1) = 4.6$, $p = .03$), while the freed direct path stays small and nonsignificant. A test with nothing to explain is easy to pass. Under a better-specified model the same restriction constrains more, so its result is more informative.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.6"}
(a) In the three-wave model the exclusion restriction passes with $\chi^2(1) = 0.36$. Why is this only weak support for the theory's claim that integration reaches disease only through the body?
(b) The autoregressive controls reduced every structural path by a factor of five or more. What feature of the outcome measures is responsible, and why does it matter for mediation specifically?
(c) Suppose integration's effect on physiology takes a decade to accumulate. What would the models of this section find, and what does that imply about the choice of lag?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.6"}
(a) A restriction is informative only when it could have failed. Integration's correlations with the disease count are close to zero in these data, so there is almost nothing for the missing direct path to explain, and nearly any model omitting it would fit. The chi-square tests the restriction given the association present; with the age-adjusted model, where the association has structure, the same restriction is nearly rejected.
(b) Hypertension and the disease count record whether a condition was *ever* diagnosed, so they can only stay level or rise, and their year-to-year stability is .82-.91. Controlling the previous wave removes all of that stable variance, leaving only new diagnoses within one year, which are rare. Mediation is a claim about transmitted *change*, so the change-based estimates are the ones the claim is about; the uncontrolled estimates largely re-describe stable differences between people.
(c) The one-year-lag paths would be nearly zero even if the theory were true, because the model looks for the effect at the wrong interval. Longitudinal effects are functions of the lag at which they are measured, and a nonsignificant lagged path is evidence against the mechanism only at that lag. Choosing the lag is a theoretical decision that the data cannot make by themselves.
:::

## Modern mediation analysis: counterfactual definitions {#sec-mediation-counterfactual}

*Optional. If you skip this section, take with you that when the model is not linear and additive, the product $\gamma_1\beta$ is not the indirect effect; the indirect effect is then defined as a counterfactual contrast and estimated by simulation, under the same no-confounding assumptions as before.*

@sec-theory-to-glm ended with a question: when the arrow into the mediator carries an ordinary regression coefficient and the arrow out of it carries a log-odds coefficient, as in the published diagram of @bayerl2024 redrawn in @fig-bayerl, what does the product of the two mean? The product multiplies numbers on different scales and has no clear interpretation. The framework above is linear; real mediation problems bring binary outcomes, interactions, and nonlinearity, and for those the modern literature defines the effects counterfactually before estimating anything [@vanderweele2016]. This literature has its own notation, which we adopt for this section: $X$ is the treatment, $M$ the mediator, $Y$ the outcome; $M(x)$ is the mediator value a person would have under treatment level $x$, and $Y(x, m)$ the outcome they would have under treatment $x$ with the mediator set to $m$. Each person has a value $Y(1, m)$ and a value $Y(0, m)$, of which at most one is ever observed, and $E[\cdot]$ denotes the average over the population, so the definitions below are averages of contrasts that no single person ever shows.

Applied papers use two definitions. The **natural direct effect** compares the outcome under treatment versus control while the mediator is held at the value it would naturally take under control ($M(0)$),

$$\text{NDE} = E[\,Y(1, M(0)) - Y(0, M(0))\,],$$

the effect that does not run through the mediator. The **natural indirect effect** holds treatment fixed and compares the outcome under the mediator value it would take with treatment versus without,

$$\text{NIE} = E[\,Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0))\,],$$

the effect that does run through the mediator. Adding the two makes the middle terms cancel, leaving $E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))]$: the total effect, a decomposition like the linear one. In the linear and additive model the NIE is exactly the coefficient product of this chapter's first section. As soon as the model departs from that form, the classic product and the counterfactual definitions differ.

The smallest departure shows the difference. Suppose treatment is 0 or 1 and the fitted equations are

$$
M = 0.5\,X + \zeta_M, \qquad
Y = 0.2\,X + 0.3\,M + 0.4\,XM + \zeta_Y,
$$

an ordinary mediation model plus one interaction term: the mediator matters more for treated units (0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7) than for controls (0.3). The classic product multiplies the treatment's effect on the mediator by the mediator's coefficient: $0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.15$. The counterfactual calculation asks instead what actually happens through the mediator when a unit is treated. Treatment raises the mediator by $E[M(1)] - E[M(0)] = 0.5$; for a treated unit, each unit of mediator is worth $0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7$; so $\text{NIE} = 0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.35$, more than twice the classic answer. (The NDE here is $0.2 + 0.4 \times E[M(0)] = 0.2$ when the untreated mediator averages zero, and $0.35 + 0.2 = 0.55$ is the total effect.)

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.7"}
Keep $Y = 0.2\,X + 0.3\,M + 0.4\,XM + \zeta_Y$, but let the mediator have a nonzero baseline: $M = 1 + 0.5\,X + \zeta_M$.

(a) Compute the NIE, the NDE and the total effect.
(b) Compute the *other* decomposition: the total direct effect $E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(1))]$, which holds the mediator at its treated value, and the pure indirect effect $E[Y(0, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))]$, which holds treatment at control. Check that these two also sum to the total effect.
(c) What does the existence of two decompositions say about "the proportion mediated"?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.7"}
(a) $E[M(0)] = 1$ and $E[M(1)] = 1.5$. NIE $= (0.3 + 0.4) \times (1.5 - 1) = 0.35$; NDE $= 0.2 + 0.4 \times E[M(0)] = 0.6$; total $= 0.95$. (As a check, $E[Y(1, M(1))] = 0.2 + 0.7 \times 1.5 = 1.25$ and $E[Y(0, M(0))] = 0.3 \times 1 = 0.3$, whose difference is $0.95$.)
(b) Total direct effect $= 0.2 + 0.4 \times E[M(1)] = 0.2 + 0.4 \times 1.5 = 0.8$; pure indirect effect $= 0.3 \times (1.5 - 1) = 0.15$; their sum is again $0.95$.
(c) The total effect is the same, but the share attributed to the mediator is $0.35/0.95 = 37$ percent under the first decomposition and $0.15/0.95 = 16$ percent under the second. With an interaction the mediator's share depends on where the interaction term is counted, so "proportion mediated" must state which decomposition it uses. In the additive model, where the interaction coefficient is zero, the two decompositions coincide and the question does not arise.
:::

The R package `mediation` computes these effects by simulation for a wide menu of models [@tingley2014], under the same no-confounding assumptions you met above, there called "sequential ignorability". A classic demonstration uses a framing experiment: participants were randomized to an anxiety-inducing immigration news story, with anxiety as the mediator and sending an anti-immigration letter to Congress as the binary outcome [@brader2008].


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mediation)
data(framing)
med.fit <- lm(emo ~ treat + age + educ + gender + income, data = framing)
out.fit <- glm(cong_mesg ~ emo + treat + age + educ + gender + income,
               data = framing, family = binomial("probit"))
set.seed(1)
med.out <- mediate(med.fit, out.fit, treat = "treat", mediator = "emo",
                   robustSE = TRUE, sims = 1000)
round(summary(med.out)$d.avg, 3)   # average causal mediation effect (NIE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.083
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(summary(med.out)$z.avg, 3)   # average direct effect (NDE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.01
```


:::
:::


The first model explains the mediator, the second the outcome; the outcome model uses a probit link, a close cousin of the logistic link of @sec-theory-to-glm that maps the linear predictor to a probability through the normal distribution instead of the logistic one. `mediate()` combines them into the average causal mediation effect (the NIE, here about 0.08 and significant) and the average direct effect (small and not significant). The treatment raised the probability of writing to Congress by about eight percentage points *through anxiety*. Because the identifying assumptions are untestable, careful papers add a sensitivity analysis, which asks how strong an unmeasured mediator-outcome confounder would have to be to explain the result away; the package computes this too, and current reporting guidelines ask for such statements.

The mediation literature pays much attention to the standard error of the indirect effect. The indirect effect $\gamma_1\beta$ is a product of two estimates, and `lavaan`'s `:=` operator, which defines a new quantity from labelled parameters (see the "Reading lavaan" box of @sec-theory-to-glm), gives its standard error in one line. For the chain model of the first simulation, whose true indirect effect is $0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.35$:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_ind <- "x2 ~ a * x1 \n x3 ~ b * x2 \n ind := a * b"
pe <- parameterEstimates(sem(m_ind, data = d))
pe[pe$op == ":=", c("label", "est", "se")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  label   est    se
6   ind 0.349 0.008
```


:::
:::


The standard error comes from the **delta method**, which approximates the variance of a function of estimates, here the product, from the variances of the estimates and the slopes of the function. Bootstrapping, which is discussed in subsequent chapters, gives nearly the same answer at ordinary sample sizes.^[The product of two normal estimates is not itself normal, which matters near zero and in small samples [@mackinnon2007]; the bootstrap handles this and is a good tool.]

## Mediation analysis is an if-then statement {#sec-mediation-if-then}

The most common misreading of a mediation analysis, and of causal analysis generally, goes like this: we fitted the mediation model, the indirect effect was significant and the model fit well, therefore we have shown that mediation occurs. This chapter's central lesson is that the "therefore" is wrong, and the equivalence result of the first failure shows why it *must* be wrong. The model with the reversed arrows fits exactly as well as the fitted one, in every dataset; so does a model in which the mediator-outcome association is pure confounding. Good fit, a significant product, and a large sample are all fully compatible with a world in which the mediation story is false. Fitting a mediation model and finding "mediation" demonstrates nothing by itself, because the same numbers would have appeared under rival stories the data cannot distinguish.

A mediation analysis delivers a conditional statement: *if* the arrows point as drawn, *if* no unmeasured common causes connect the mediator and the outcome, and, where an instrument is used, *if* the exclusion restriction holds, *then* the estimates quantify the mediation process. The analysis converts assumptions into conclusions and cannot supply the assumptions itself. Whether the if-clauses are plausible is settled outside the model, by the design: randomization secures the cause's arrows, temporal ordering in panel data secures part of the causal order (while leaving confounding and the choice of lag untouched), an instrument trades one untestable assumption for another, and a cross-sectional survey secures almost none of it. The same fitted model therefore supports a strong claim in one design and almost no claim in another, and no estimator, sample size, or software can substitute for the missing clauses: identification is a property of the question-design pair. When you meet an analysis, ask the fifth of the five questions of @sec-rq-to-interpretation: what in the design put the answer to this question into the data? If nothing did, no estimator can recover it. Papers that claim mediation because the model fit are asserting the *then* without having established the *if*.

## What to carry forward {.unnumbered}

A mediation model is the practice model of @sec-theory-to-glm read causally, and the decomposition rule splits the total effect into a direct effect $\gamma_2$ and an indirect effect $\gamma_1\beta$; reading them causally requires that nothing confounds cause and mediator, nothing confounds mediator and outcome, and the arrows point the way drawn, and randomizing the cause secures only the first of these (@sec-mediation-model, @sec-mediation-assumptions). Two models are equivalent when they imply the same distribution of observable data, and a question is identified when that distribution determines its answer (@def-identification); the reversed chain fits exactly as well as the true one, and a hidden common cause of mediator and outcome produces a precise, significant and wrong $\hat\beta$, so fit and sample size cannot settle either question and only design can (@sec-failure-reversed, @sec-failure-confounder). An instrumental variable trades the assumption of no mediator-outcome confounding for the exclusion restriction, and the effect is then the ratio $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$, the Wald estimator, which needs relevance, exclusion and exogeneity and becomes erratic when the instrument is weak (@sec-iv, @sec-iv-practice). Panel data secure part of the causal order and, with autoregressive paths, ask whether the cause predicts *change* in the mediator, which is the question a mediation theory poses; confounding and the choice of lag remain untouched (@sec-mediation-panel). When the model is not linear and additive, the indirect effect is defined as a counterfactual contrast, the natural indirect effect, and the product $\gamma_1\beta$ no longer equals it (@sec-mediation-counterfactual). Every mediation result is an if-then statement whose if-clauses the design must supply; @sec-evaluation and @sec-unsupervised use this conditional reading of a fitted model, and @sec-unsupervised returns to identification for latent variables (@sec-mediation-if-then).

**Terms and symbols introduced.** mediation; equivalent models; identified; exclusion restriction; instrumental variable; intention-to-treat effect; Wald estimator; two-stage least squares; relevance, exclusion, exogeneity; attenuation; encouragement design; Mendelian randomization; compliers; local average treatment effect; autoregressive path; suppression; natural direct effect, natural indirect effect; delta method; $\psi$ the covariance between the disturbances of mediator and outcome, $M(x)$ the mediator value under treatment $x$, $Y(x, m)$ the outcome under treatment $x$ with the mediator set to $m$, $E[\cdot]$ the population average, $a$, $b$, $c'$ the Baron–Kenny names for $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, $\gamma_2$.

## Further study {.unnumbered}

@angrist2009 is the econometric treatment of instrumental variables, with weak instruments, two-stage least squares and the local average treatment effect worked out in full, and @angrist1996 is the paper that defines compliers and the local effect and connects instruments to the potential-outcome notation of the optional section. @vanderweele2016 is a short guide to the counterfactual definitions of direct and indirect effects and to the sensitivity analyses that careful mediation papers now report; @vanderweele2015 is the book-length version, with binary outcomes, interactions and the identification assumptions treated in full. @mackinnon2007 reviews the psychological mediation literature, including the standard error of the indirect effect and the bootstrap. @bullock2010 and @rohrer2022 are the critiques of mediation practice in psychology summarized in this chapter, and are the papers to read before writing a mediation section of your own. @cole2003 and @maxwell2007 are the sources for the longitudinal design and for the bias of cross-sectional mediation estimates when the process unfolds over time. @pearl2009 gives the graphical theory in which identification, equivalence and instruments have general definitions.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.A"}
An abstract reads: "Whether living near a fast-food outlet causes obesity is disputed, since outlets choose their locations. We exploit the fact that highway service areas host fast-food outlets for reasons unrelated to local residents' health. Among 130,000 residents of towns at varying distances from service areas, we use highway proximity as an instrument for fast-food exposure and estimate its effect on body mass index."

(a) Identify the three variables in the instrumental-variable triangle and draw the assumed diagram, including the correlated disturbances.
(b) The abstract has four sentences. Say which of the three instrument conditions (relevance, exclusion, exogeneity) each sentence asserts, if any.
(c) Suppose highway proximity also brings traffic noise and air pollution, which affect health. Which condition fails, and what happens to the estimate?
(d) Suppose fast-food outlets near highways serve the same food as elsewhere, but residents near highways rarely eat out at all, so proximity barely shifts exposure. Which condition fails, and what happens to the estimate?
(e) A colleague proposes to fix problem (c) by controlling for measured air quality. What assumption does the fix require?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.A"}
(a) $\xi$ = highway proximity (instrument), $\eta_1$ = fast-food exposure, $\eta_2$ = BMI; arrows $\xi \rightarrow \eta_1 \rightarrow \eta_2$, curved arrow between the disturbances of $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$, no direct $\xi \rightarrow \eta_2$ path. (b) The first sentence asserts none of the conditions; it states the confounding problem (outlets' location choices are a common cause of exposure and BMI) that makes an instrument necessary. The second asserts exogeneity: service areas are placed for reasons unrelated to residents' health, so proximity shares no common cause with BMI. The third asserts relevance: proximity shifts exposure, and towns at varying distances supply the variation, although the abstract asserts this rather than reports the first-stage strength. The fourth asserts exclusion, but only implicitly: reading the estimate as "the effect of exposure" requires that proximity reaches BMI through exposure alone, and no sentence says so. That silence is typical, and part (c) is about exactly this condition. (c) Exclusion: pollution and noise are direct paths from proximity to BMI that bypass exposure, so $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta + \text{direct part}$ and the ratio no longer isolates $\beta$; the estimate absorbs the pollution effect. (d) Relevance: $\gamma_1 \approx 0$, the denominator is near zero, and the estimator becomes wildly unstable (and any small exclusion violation is amplified). (e) That air quality is measured well enough, and that after controlling for it no *other* direct path from proximity to BMI remains; the exclusion restriction is repaired only as far as the controls are complete, which is an assumption, not a test result.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.B"}
A published paper reports, from a cross-sectional survey of 2,000 office workers: "Job insecurity predicted burnout ($\beta = 0.21$). This effect was fully mediated by sleep quality ($ab = 0.19$, bootstrap 95% CI [0.12, 0.27]); the direct effect was not significant. We conclude that insecure employment burns people out by disrupting their sleep, and that sleep interventions can undo this harm."

(a) List the assumptions this conclusion requires, and label each as supported or unsupported by the design.
(b) Construct a concrete rival world, with the same fitted numbers, in which sleep interventions would achieve nothing.
(c) The authors emphasize the bootstrap confidence interval. Evaluate, in one or two sentences, how much that emphasis adds.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.B"}
(a) Correct causal order (insecurity $\rightarrow$ sleep $\rightarrow$ burnout): unsupported; all three variables were measured at once, and burnt-out workers may sleep badly and judge their job prospects more pessimistically. No insecurity-sleep confounding and no sleep-burnout confounding: unsupported; a failing employer, say, plausibly causes insecurity, late nights, and exhaustion at once. Linearity and additivity: conventional. (b) Let the employer's decline drive insecurity, poor sleep, and burnout, with no arrow from sleep to burnout at all: the three correlations can reproduce the published coefficients, yet improving sleep changes nothing because sleep never caused the burnout. (c) Very little. The bootstrap gives a valid interval around $ab$, but the number it brackets is causal only under the assumptions in (a), and a narrow interval does not make those assumptions more plausible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.C"}
A Mendelian randomization study uses a variant that slows alcohol metabolism as an instrument for alcohol consumption, with esophageal cancer as the outcome.

(a) State the three instrument conditions in genetic terms.
(b) The variant also causes facial flushing, which affects social behaviour and stress; through which condition does this threaten the analysis, and what is the term of art?
(c) The variant is common in East Asian populations and rare elsewhere, and populations differ in diet. Explain the resulting bias and one design remedy.
(d) In what precise sense does even a successful analysis answer a "local" question?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.C"}
(a) Relevance: the variant shifts consumption. Exogeneity: the variant is dealt independently of confounders of drinking and cancer, the meiotic lottery. Exclusion: the variant affects cancer only through consumption. (b) Exclusion; a second pathway from gene to outcome is "pleiotropy". (c) Ancestry is a common cause of carrying the variant and of dietary exposures: confounding of the instrument itself, called population stratification. Remedies: analyse within genetically homogeneous groups, adjust for measured ancestry (in practice, a handful of summary scores computed from the whole genome that capture where a person's ancestors came from), or use within-family designs, where the lottery argument holds exactly. (d) The estimate reflects the effect of consumption among people whose drinking the variant actually shifts, the compliers; heavy drinkers who would drink regardless contribute nothing, so extrapolation to them is an extra assumption [@angrist1996; @deaton2010].
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.D (optional)"}
This last exercise is optional: it works out what a small violation of the exclusion restriction does to the instrumental-variable estimate, and it is more challenging than the others. Nothing later in the book depends on it.

Suppose the exclusion restriction fails slightly: $\eta_2 = \beta\,\eta_1 + \gamma_2\,\xi + \zeta_2$ with a small direct effect $\gamma_2$, while the instrument is still exogenous and the disturbances are still correlated.

(a) Using the decomposition rule, show that the IV ratio $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$ converges to $\beta + \gamma_2/\gamma_1$ rather than to $\beta$.
(b) Evaluate the bias for $\gamma_2 = 0.02$ with a strong instrument ($\gamma_1 = 0.5$) and with a weak one ($\gamma_1 = 0.05$), and compare it with a naive estimate whose confounding bias is $\psi = 0.2$.
(c) Modify `one_iv` from Exercise 3.4 so that `Y` contains `0.02 * X`, run 2,000 replicates at each instrument strength, and report the median estimate. (Why the median rather than the mean? Look back at Exercise 3.4(b).)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.D"}
(a) With the direct path present, $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$ as before, but $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta + \gamma_2$: the direct effect joins the indirect effect, and neither equation contains $\psi$. The ratio is $(\gamma_1\beta + \gamma_2)/\gamma_1 = \beta + \gamma_2/\gamma_1$. The exclusion violation is divided by the instrument's strength.
(b) Strong instrument: $0.02/0.5 = 0.04$. Weak instrument: $0.02/0.05 = 0.40$, twice the confounding bias of $0.2$ that the naive estimate had. A weak instrument turns a small exclusion violation into a large bias, which is the point of @bound1995: the two conditions interact, and a weak instrument makes the exclusion restriction matter more, not less.
(c) Change the line for `Y` to `Y <- 0.02 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)` and run `median(replicate(2000, one_iv(0.5)))` and the same with `one_iv(0.05)`. The strong-instrument median is about $0.04$, as in (b). The weak-instrument median is about $0.37$, a little below the limit of $0.40$, because with an instrument this weak 1,000 observations are not yet a large sample; it moves between about $0.34$ and $0.40$ from one seed to the next. The median is used because the weak-instrument distribution has the heavy tails of Exercise 3.4(b): individual replicates land in the hundreds, of either sign, and the mean of 2,000 of them is dominated by a few of those.
:::
